note: Interstate competition, fiscal resources and military innovation form a tournament explanation of European expansion. Comparisons with other regions add boundary conditions; counterfactual attribution remains less secure than documented military investment. Not a technical curriculum or advocacy of conquest. Military domination central, T12 applies; stated expansion period ends 1914.

Ottoman institutions, dynastic struggles and administrative adaptation explain a transcontinental empire across six centuries. Long chronological detail lowers strategic density but does not remove transferable mechanisms. Imperial political power central, T12 applies; multinational scope is not treated as one modern nation's history. Empire's final transition ends 1923; original 2005 publication precedes 2006 US edition.

author: Faramerz Dabhoiwala
note: Early modern changes in sexual regulation connect religion, law, print culture and personal freedoms. Distinct institutions add explanation rather than advice about sex or doctrinal truth. Primarily British development warrants T11 despite wider Western influence. Historical arc ends around 1800. Weak domain fit, but explanatory payload is present.

Afghan and imperial sources explain occupation, legitimacy failures, logistics and rebellion. Multiple perspectives add evidence and strategic constraints; detailed campaign narrative reduces direct yield for this reader. International conflict, T11 zero; military intervention central, T12 applies. First Anglo-Afghan War ends 1842.

Dictator-centered cases connect resource rents, foreign commercial interests and patronage. Those mechanisms prevent V3, despite personality-heavy narrative and limited technical content. Political figures and power predominate, both thematic deductions. Multiple regimes across periods have no one historical endpoint; contemporary reporting limits durability.

Continuity planning links communications, bunkers, command arrangements and institutional incentives under nuclear risk. Different failure modes give transferable resilience lessons; operational anecdote and secrecy limit certainty. US government/military planning central, both thematic deductions. Program history extends into ongoing present rather than a single closed episode.

author: James L. Stokesbury
title: A Short History of World War I
note: Concise multi-front history connects causes, campaigns, technology and consequences. Cross-front comparisons add explanation beyond battle lists, though strategic mechanisms are less developed than narrative. International scope, no single-nation deduction. War central, T12 applies; endpoint 1918.

Archival history connects collectivization, coercive extraction, political decisions and famine. Policy mechanisms provide transferable lessons despite unwanted subject. Ukraine-focused Stalin-era political violence warrants both thematic deductions; central famine endpoint 1933. Documented endnotes 368–436 plus bibliography 437–453 form 86 pages; no index counted. Interpretation of intent remains distinct from documentation of mortality and state actions.

Global treatment connects European campaigns to trade, colonial theaters, diplomacy and state resources. Additional regions contribute real historical constraints rather than simple repetition, supporting length provisionally. War central, T12 applies; international scope avoids T11. Endpoint 1815. Library documents bibliographical-reference span 642–883; 242 pages counted, index excluded.

author: Tomás Mandl
note: Country study combines modern politics, economy and society to explain Paraguay's development. Some institutional transfer remains, so low fit is not V3. Mixed overview and local detail imply moderate learning yield, low confidence. Single-nation political account warrants both deductions. Broad history to contemporary conditions, no one central closed period.

author: Milton Leitenberg; Raymond A. Zilinskas; Jens H. Kuhn
note: Interviews and archival records explain a secret weapons research organization, resources, incentives and verification problems. Institutional history, not biological-weapons procedures. Different institutes and decision failures add learning; uncertain post-Soviet remnants are not treated as proven continuity. Soviet national program and military aims warrant both deductions. Central program endpoint approximately 1992; later uncertainty does not erase topic-age deduction.

Geography, colonial institutions, economic performance and identity explain a fragmented state. Comparative development and geopolitical context prevent V3 despite strong national focus. Different historical layers add learning. Philippines-centered state and political history warrants both deductions; broad trajectory through the present has no single closed period.

Multinational archives explain decolonization, coalition decisions and escalation from France's war toward US involvement in Vietnam. Missed alternatives and institutional commitments provide transfer, so no V3. Vietnam/American-tragedy framing and war central, both deductions apply. Approximate main narrative endpoint 1959. Rich cases may earn length, with extensive diplomatic narrative reducing density for this reader.

Text formation, transmission, canon and interpretation are studied historically. The author being a priest does not establish V5 or V8; the stated central purpose is literary history rather than proving doctrine. Different textual traditions add substantive distinctions. Low domain fit remains included. Cross-period history without one central endpoint; no philosophy deduction merely for historical religious material.

author: Cathal J. Nolan
note: Comparative military history contrasts decisive-battle narratives with endurance, logistics, resources and coalition capacity. Different wars supply constraints and counterexamples rather than automatic padding. Broad explanatory thesis remains historical interpretation, not a proven universal law. Military history central, T12 applies; broad cross-period comparison gives H13 zero.
